doctrine: Transcript of AlphaGo documentary (DeepMind/Google production). Core substance: (1) Game as AI training platform: Go's 10^170 possible board states makes brute-force computation impossible; intuition-mimicking neural networks required. (2) AlphaGo architecture: policy network (imitates human moves), value network (evaluates board positions), tree search (evaluates variations). (3) Paradigm shift in creative problem-solving: Move 37 (5th-line shoulder hit, 1-in-10,000 human probability) and Move 78 (wedge sacrifice) demonstrated AI can generate novel tactics outside training data. (4) Human-AI collaboration insight: AlphaGo's 'slack moves' teach humans that winning by 1 point equals winning by 100 points; margins don't determine victory probability. (5) AlphaGo's vulnerability: gets 'delusional' in unfamiliar positions, can search too deeply and lose coherence; Lee Sedol exploited this in Game 4. (6) Emotional/cultural weight: Go as mirror to player's mind; loss reframed from humiliation to accelerated mastery. (7) Historical parallel: Deep Blue vs Kasparov (chess, 1997) established that human intuition could be replicated; AlphaGo (2016, Go) proved it could be exceeded AND teach humans new game theory.
workflows: DeepMind 2-year AlphaGo development cycle before Lee Sedol match
Fan Hui (European champion) test-matches, then recruited as advisor post-loss
5-game match structure with media/commentary infrastructure in Seoul
Post-game analysis loops: identifying weaknesses, version iteration (v18), reinforcement learning via self-play
prompts: How can we train a neural network to play Go without telling it the rules?
What does it mean when a machine finds a move humans would never consider?
Can AlphaGo's creativity teach us something about human intuition?
tools: Real-time evaluation metrics (win probability, search depth)
operating_rules: Train on 100,000 human games first (imitation), then iterate via self-play (no human input needed after)
AlphaGo maximizes win probability, not margin of victory (teaches 'slack moves')
Search depth 50-60 moves ahead typical; deeper searches can trigger delusions/errors
Policy network + value net + tree search = better intuition simulation than pure calculation
Weakness in novel/unfamiliar positions: mistakes when evaluating board states it hasn't seen in training
content_ideas: Move 37 and Move 78 as examples of creative outputs beyond training data
Lee Sedol's psychological journey: humiliation > acceptance > mastery
Go's cultural weight in Korea as national identity vs. AI milestone
The 'delusion' phenomenon: when AlphaGo's search becomes incoherent under complexity
Slack moves: new economic theory of game play (minimum margin = maximum efficiency)
contradictions: AlphaGo billed as 'learning itself' yet heavily trained on human games first; not purely self-taught
Move 37 described as 'creative breakthrough' yet commentators later note AlphaGo knew it was a 1-in-10,000 move (suggesting calculation, not creativity in human sense)
Claims AlphaGo couldn't be beaten, but Game 4 Lee Sedol win proves it has exploitable weaknesses (unclear if these are permanent or version-dependent)
Anthropomorphization risk: commentators and audience treating AlphaGo as 'he/she' despite being deterministic code; emotional narratives overlay on mechanical process
weird_gold: Fan Hui's postmatch breakdown and reentry: 'I am not happy to lose the game, but I will be happy for play in the history' sets template for redemptive framing
Lee Sedol's Game 4 win felt by crowd as 'we can still hold our own' / national survival moment despite being one game out of five

Kasparov Deep Blue parallel (lines 430-446): chess had 'multiple approaches to solving intellectual problems'; Go was supposed harder, yet fell in same timeframe (industry predictions: decades, actual: ~12 years)
Frank's 'slack move' insight reframes all of Go history: 'lessons will influence how Go is played for the next thousand years' based on single machine preference pattern
Aja Huang (AlphaGo's move executor) simultaneously proud and anxious; his physical body mediates human-machine interface; crowd watches his expressions for signs
Move 37 aftermath: professional Go community immediately recognized impossibility; players began studying AlphaGo's 'mistakes' as advanced technique
